Claude Code: request flow and controls

The step-by-step guide explains each step in general; how to read these trees.

What happens to a request

The steps run in the typical order. A documented order, where the vendor states one, is shown on its step. A decision point appears where the documentation describes a real branch; an agent with none has none documented.

A. Setup, before the first model call

The harness gets ready: it finds your rules, your tools and your permissions. No model is involved yet.

  1. Choose the front door ◐ documented, with limits !

    You can use it in a terminal, in IDEs such as VS Code, in a desktop app, on the web, from scripts and through CI or chat tools. In script mode Claude doesn't spawn teammates, the desktop hand-off needs a Mac or Windows computer, and repository setup works only with github.com.

  2. Apply organization rules ◐ documented, with limits !

    A company can set rules for its developers' installs: which tools and commands are allowed or denied, which models are offered, and whether background agents run. Managed rules win over options set in code. Claude Tag cloud sessions don't receive server-managed settings.

    Documented order: Managed policy settings win over options set in code.

  3. Load the house rules ● documented !

    It reads instruction files from your project and home folder at the start of a session and adds their text to every request. Files at all levels contribute at once, and Claude uses judgment when they conflict. Files can import other files, up to four hops deep.

    Documented order: Broader locations load first, so a project instruction appears after a user instruction.

    Decision point: When does a rules file get loaded?

    • The rule has no paths list: It loads at the start of the session, alongside the main instruction file.

      Rules without paths: frontmatter load at session start

    • The rule has a paths list: It loads only when Claude reads, writes or edits a file that matches.

      a rule with YAML paths: frontmatter loads only when Claude reads, writes, or edits a matching file

    Documented in F03.path-scoped-rules. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  4. Load memory and earlier sessions ◐ documented, with limits !

    Claude can keep notes between sessions, and you can resume, rename, branch or export earlier conversations, which are saved locally. Handoff from the command line is one-way: you can pull a cloud session into the terminal, but can't push a terminal session to the cloud.

  5. Stock the built-in tools ◐ documented, with limits !

    It ships tools for running shell commands, reading, editing and writing files, searching, fetching web pages and starting subagents. Web search is not available on Amazon Bedrock. Shell commands have a default timeout that can be raised up to a cap.

  6. Load skills and custom commands ● documented !

    You add reusable instructions as skills, which Claude loads in full only when it uses one, or as commands you type yourself. They live in set folders or come from plugins, and skills are the recommended way to package multi-step commands. A skill can set its own tools and model.

    Documented order: If an added directory and the project define a command with the same name, the project's command runs.

    Decision point: How does Claude learn about and use a skill?

    • A skill with default settings: Claude sees it in a list of available skills; its full content loads only when Claude uses it.

      full skill content loads only when Claude uses one

    • A skill that blocks model invocation: It is left out of that list and stays out of context until you invoke it by name.

      Skills with disable-model-invocation: true are not in that list and stay out of context until you invoke them with /name

    Documented in F08.invocation. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  7. Connect outside tools ◐ documented, with limits !

    You connect outside programs through MCP servers, which add extra tools that need explicit permission. Project servers need a one-time approval and administrators can restrict which servers users add. Consent dialogs don't relay: they only appear in the local terminal.

  8. Set the safety posture ◐ documented, with limits !

    Modes range from plan, which explores without editing source files, through manual and accept-edits to auto and bypass. Manual asks before editing but can change files once you approve. Desktop remembers a mode per folder, except plan, which lasts for the session.

    Documented order: In Desktop, a mode picked for a folder wins over the default mode setting for that folder.

    Decision point: What happens in a folder I have not trusted yet?

    • Trust not yet accepted for the folder: A workspace trust dialog appears; accepting saves trust for the workspace.

      If workspace trust hasn't been accepted for a directory, Claude Code shows the workspace trust dialog

    • An agent file sits in an untrusted folder: A teammate gets that agent's tools and instructions only if you trusted that folder; trusting a parent folder doesn't count.

      A teammate gets an agent definition's tools and instructions only if you've trusted the folder the agent file is in

    Documented in F04.trust-prompt. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  9. Pick the model and thinking effort ◐ documented, with limits

    You pick a model with a picker, a setting or a command option, and set effort per session or by default. It connects to Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Google Cloud and gateways. Foundry has no startup model check, so requests fail if the default is unavailable.

  10. Prepare an isolated workspace ● documented !

    It can give each session its own separate copy of your project in a worktree, so parallel sessions don't edit the same files. Each copy sits on its own branch, and the repository needs at least one commit first.

B. Each turn, before sending

For every request the harness decides what the model will read, and runs any code you asked it to run first.

  1. Assemble the prompt ● documented !

    The context window holds the system instructions, tool definitions, the conversation and tool results. Some models support a 1 million token window. Some tools load on demand, and a subagent's intermediate work stays inside it, so just its final message returns.

  2. Run your own code at set moments ◐ documented, with limits !

    Hooks run a script, request, prompt or subagent at set moments and can allow, deny or change a tool call. A hook's allow doesn't skip deny and ask rules. Some hooks exist in one SDK only, and non-interactive runs without the bare option use project hooks in untrusted folders.

    Documented order: A PreToolUse hook runs before the rest of the permission flow.

    Decision point: Do hooks run without asking me first?

    • Hooks come from managed settings: Interactive users see a security approval dialog before the hooks are applied.

      interactive users see a security approval dialog before Claude Code applies them

    • Print-mode run without the bare option: Project hooks run even in an untrusted folder, with no workspace trust dialog.

      a -p session runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json, even in a folder you've never trusted

    • The settings option disables hooks: Hooks are switched off for that run.

      Passing --settings with disableAllHooks set to true

    Documented in F06.trust-enable. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

C. The model call

The harness sends the request and waits. This is the only step where the model itself does any work.

  1. Send the request and handle trouble ● documented !

    If the main model is overloaded or unavailable, a session with a backup model set switches to it and retries the main one at the start of each turn. When a usage limit blocks a request, a command shows ways to keep working, such as waiting for the reset or adding credits.

    Documented order: After switching to the backup, the main model is retried at the start of each user turn.

    Decision point: How does it switch models on its own?

    • Main model overloaded, backup set: The session switches to the backup model and retries the main one at the start of each user turn.

      a session with fallbackModel set switches to the backup and retries the primary at the start of each user turn

    • Plan-then-execute choice in plan mode: It applies during plan mode if the allowed-models list permits, then switches to Sonnet for execution.

      opusplan applies during plan mode when allowed by availableModels, then switches to Sonnet for execution

    • A subagent has no model set: It follows the subagent model order.

      Omitted subagent models follow the subagent model order

    Documented in F17.auto-routing. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  2. Set the thinking budget ◐ documented, with limits

    Extended thinking is on by default, its tokens are billed as output, and the reasoning shows as gray italic text in the terminal. Not all models support effort levels, and the thinking token cap applies on models with a fixed thinking budget.

  3. Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt · not researched not yet researched

D. After the model answers, every turn

The model's answer is only a request. The harness checks it, runs it if allowed, and feeds the result back.

  1. Read what the model asked for · not researched not yet researched
  2. Decide whether it is allowed ◐ documented, with limits !

    Rules allow, ask or deny specific tools, and can be narrowed by path or by command. Command rules match the literal command text, so a deny on one form doesn't block another route to the same effect. In auto mode a model classifier blocks irreversible or destructive actions.

  3. Save an undo point ◐ documented, with limits

    Pressing Esc twice, or using the rewind command, opens a menu to restore an earlier conversation and code state. Checkpoints don't track files changed by shell commands, and snapshots are kept for the 100 most recent checkpoints.

  4. Run it inside the fence ◐ documented, with limits !

    Shell commands can run in a sandbox that limits which files they change and which network addresses they reach. It covers shell commands and their child processes, but hooks and MCP servers run outside it, and some commands are excluded or can fall back to running unsandboxed.

    Decision point: When can a command run outside the sandbox?

    • The command is on the excluded list: It runs unsandboxed automatically, without the model being involved.

      bypass sandbox restrictions and run unsandboxed automatically without model involvement

    • The sandbox can't start and failing is turned off: It falls back to running without a sandbox and prints a warning.

      falls back to unsandboxed execution with a warning on stderr when the sandbox can't start

    • You type it at the shell-mode prompt: It runs unsandboxed in most sessions.

      Commands typed at the `!` shell-mode prompt run unsandboxed in most sessions

    Documented in F05.sandbox-override. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  5. Tidy the tool's output · not researched not yet researched
  6. Feed the result back and go round again ◐ documented, with limits

    A turn runs from a prompt to a response. Read-only tools can run at the same time, while tools that change state run one after another. The command-line turn limit works in print mode only and has no limit by default, and a session doesn't time out on its own.

  7. Hand work to helpers ◐ documented, with limits !

    It can hand work to helper agents with their own instructions, tools and model, and run several at once, up to 20 by default. The documentation differs on nesting: one page says helpers can start their own helpers, another says by default they lack the tool for it.

    Documented order: A subagent's own effort setting wins over the session's effort level.

  8. Shrink the context when it fills ● documented !

    When the conversation nears the context limit, Claude Code compacts it automatically, keeping important code and decisions. You can also compact by hand and give instructions on what to focus on.

  9. Show the answer or ask you ● documented

    Plan mode explores and plans without editing source files, and file edits there are never auto-approved. A status line at the bottom can be customized, and a status command shows the API provider and the auto mode server state.

  10. Wrap up and keep score ◐ documented, with limits !

    It shows usage and cost totals, can export metrics to your own monitoring stack, and writes debug logs. A spending cap exists, but on the command line it works in print mode only, and the SDK cap ignores totals restored from a resumed session.

E. Around the session

Things that sit outside a single turn: unattended runs, add-ons, updates and who runs the service.

  1. Run without you watching ◐ documented, with limits !

    It can run in the background, on a schedule, in the cloud, or react to outside events such as a failed CI run. To involve a different tool you expose it through MCP, and in every approach the workers are Claude sessions.

  2. Extend and share ◐ documented, with limits !

    A plugin bundles skills, hooks, helper agents and MCP servers into one installable unit. Agents shipped in a plugin honor a subset of the subagent fields, and a shared marketplace list applies only after each teammate trusts the folder.

  3. Updates and releases ● documented !

    It has a stable and a latest release channel, updates itself or by hand, and shows its changelog in the app. The documentation marks removed and renamed options, and says breaking gateway protocol changes are announced in advance, though indefinite compatibility isn't guaranteed.

  4. Where it runs and who runs it ◐ documented, with limits

    The same engine runs in the terminal, editors, Desktop and the web, and plan usage is shared across them. If a host platform embeds it, Claude Code ignores its own provider settings. An API key, when set, is used instead of your subscription.

  5. Identity, retention and audit ◐ documented, with limits !

    Organizations can require single sign-on, restrict login to a method or organization, and export usage metrics. The default retention period is 30 days, the minimum is 1, and setting 0 is rejected with an error.
